# Drum Machines

Two failed products from Roland became the rhythmic foundation of nearly all
modern popular music.

---

## Roland TR-808 (1980–1983)

**Type:** fully **analog** drum synthesiser. Every sound is generated by
circuits, not samples. It was designed to imitate real drums, failed at that
completely, sold about 12,000 units, and was discontinued.

### How each voice works

| Voice | Circuit | Key control |
|---|---|---|
| **Bass drum** | A **bridged-T oscillator** rung by a trigger pulse — a sine that decays | **Decay** (up to ~2 s), **Tone** |
| **Snare** | Two bridged-T oscillators (~180 Hz and ~330 Hz) + filtered noise | **Snappy** (noise vs body balance), **Tone** |
| **Cowbell** | Two square-wave oscillators (~540 Hz and ~800 Hz) through a band-pass | Level only |
| **Claves / rimshot** | A single ringing bridged-T | Level |
| **Hi-hats / cymbal** | **Six square-wave oscillators** at inharmonic frequencies through a high-pass | **Decay** (CH/OH), **Tone** |
| **Toms / congas** | Bridged-T with a pitch envelope | **Tuning** |
| **Handclap** | A burst of noise gated by several fast pulses, then a longer noise tail | Level |

### The bass drum is the whole story
Turn the **Decay** control up and the 808 kick becomes a **sustained sine tone at
about 50 Hz** lasting up to two seconds. It is no longer a drum: it is a bass
note. That single design choice, plus the fact that it can be tuned, created
the 808 bass of Miami bass, Southern hip-hop and — three decades later — trap.

### What it changed
Afrika Bambaataa "Planet Rock" (1982), Marvin Gaye "Sexual Healing" (1982),
Whitney Houston "I Wanna Dance With Somebody", the whole of Miami bass, acid
house, Detroit techno, and every trap record made since 2005. Probably the most
influential drum machine ever built.

### Rebuild
```
KICK:    sine, pitch 100→50 Hz over 20-40 ms, exponential decay 200 ms-2 s,
         optional soft clip. Tune it to the track's root note.
SNARE:   two sines (180 and 330 Hz, decay 100 ms) + band-passed noise
         (1-8 kHz, decay 150 ms), balance = "snappy"
CLAP:    3-4 noise bursts 8-12 ms apart (each ~10 ms, band-pass 1-3 kHz),
         then a decaying noise tail of 200 ms
COWBELL: two square waves at 540 and 800 Hz, band-passed 800 Hz-6 kHz,
         decay 100-400 ms, no pitch envelope
HATS:    six squares at inharmonic ratios (e.g. 1, 1.34, 1.61, 1.99, 2.44, 2.79
         × ~320 Hz) through a high-pass at 6-8 kHz;
         closed decay 30-60 ms, open decay 300-600 ms
TOMS:    sine with a pitch drop over 60 ms, decay 300-600 ms
```

---

## Roland TR-909 (1983–1984)

**Type:** **hybrid** — analog kick, snare, toms, rimshot and clap; **6-bit
sampled** hi-hats, crash and ride. Also a commercial disappointment (about
10,000 sold).

### Why it sounds different from the 808
| | 808 | 909 |
|---|---|---|
| Kick | Pure sine, long, no attack | Sine with a **pitch envelope and a distinct click transient** |
| Snare | Two tones + noise, thin | Noisier, brighter, more aggressive |
| Hats | Analog squares, metallic | **Sampled**, 6-bit, splashy and gritty |
| Feel | Deep, warm, sub-heavy | Punchy, driving, mid-forward |

The 909's kick has **attack** — a click and a fast downward pitch sweep — which
is exactly what a four-on-the-floor track needs to drive. The 808's kick has
**weight** but no attack, which is what hip-hop needs.

### What it changed
**House and techno.** The 909 kick, clap and open hat are the literal sound of
the genre — the offbeat 909 open hat is the single most recognisable element in
dance music. Also the accent/velocity per step, and its "shuffle" control.

### Rebuild
```
KICK:  sine, pitch 220→55 Hz over 15-30 ms (this fast sweep IS the 909),
       decay 200-400 ms, plus a 2-5 ms noise/click layer at 2-4 kHz,
       drive into soft clipping
SNARE: noise (band-pass 200 Hz-10 kHz, decay 120 ms) + two tones at 200/280 Hz,
       heavily noise-weighted, bright
CLAP:  as the 808 but brighter and with a longer, noisier tail
OH:    band-passed noise + metallic square stack, decay 300-500 ms,
       6-bit quantised, sample rate reduced to ~25 kHz
```

## Roland CR-78 (1978)

Preset rhythm box (rock, bossa, waltz…) with a few user-programmable slots and
a beautifully soft, woody sound. Heard on Blondie's "Heart of Glass", Phil
Collins's "In the Air Tonight", Ultravox. The sound of "warm, cheap, slightly
toy-like drum machine".

---

## Linn LM-1 (1980) and LinnDrum (1982)

**Type:** the **first drum machine using digital samples of real drums**.
8-bit, individually tunable, with individual outputs.

Two innovations that outlived the machine:
1. **Real drum samples** — this is why 80s records have recognisable snare and
   tom sounds rather than synthesised approximations.
2. **Swing/shuffle quantisation** — Roger Linn's implementation defined how
   every subsequent machine and DAW does groove.

The LM-1 had no cymbals (memory cost). Prince used one on almost everything;
Human League, Michael Jackson ("Thriller" uses a LinnDrum alongside live drums),
The Cars, and much of 80s pop.

**Rebuild:** 8-bit truncated drum samples, individually tuned by varispeed, with
swing applied to the offbeat 16ths.

---

## Oberheim DMX (1980)

The LinnDrum's competitor, and hip-hop's preferred machine: Run-DMC, Kurtis
Blow, New Order ("Blue Monday" uses a DMX alongside other machines), Davy DMX.
Punchier and more aggressive than the Linn.

---

## Roland TR-707 / 727 (1985)

All-PCM, no analog voices, cheap. Thin and clicky in a way that became useful:
Chicago house and early techno used them extensively, and the 707's dry,
lifeless samples cut through club systems.

---

## Simmons SDS-V (1981)

Hexagonal electronic drum pads with analog synthesis. **The 80s electronic tom**
— a pitch-swept, noisy "pew" — is a Simmons. Heard on almost every 1983–1986
pop record.

**Rebuild:** a triangle or sine with a fast downward pitch sweep over 200–400 ms,
mixed with noise, through a resonant low-pass, with a click at the start.

---

## E-mu Drumulator / Alesis HR-16 / Yamaha RX5

The affordable 80s samplers-of-drums. The HR-16 in particular is on a lot of
early industrial, EBM and house records because it was cheap and its samples
were dry and hard.

---

## Roland TR-8S, Elektron Machinedrum / Digitakt, and the modern era

- **Elektron Machinedrum** (2001) — multiple synthesis engines per voice plus
  **parameter locks** (a different parameter value on every step). Parameter
  locking is arguably the most important sequencing idea since swing.
- **Elektron Digitakt / Rytm** — the modern sampling drum machines; p-locks,
  conditional trigs, retrigs.
- **Roland TR-8S** — modelled 808/909/707 plus samples.

### Parameter locks — worth stealing
Instead of one sound with one setting, **every step of the sequence can have a
different value for any parameter**: pitch, decay, filter, sample choice. A
16-step hi-hat line with a different decay and pitch on each step sounds alive
in a way no velocity curve achieves.

---

## Choosing a drum machine sound

| Want | Use |
|---|---|
| Deep sub weight, no attack | 808 kick with long decay, tuned |
| Driving four-to-the-floor | 909 kick with a fast pitch sweep and a click |
| Warm, soft, retro | CR-78 |
| Recognisable 80s pop | LinnDrum / DMX (8-bit real samples) |
| Dry, hard, cheap club | TR-707 |
| 80s electronic toms | Simmons |
| Gritty golden-age hip-hop | SP-1200 (12-bit, chopped) |
| Modern, evolving, per-step variety | Parameter locks on anything |
